**Section III: Comprehension (10 marks)**

Read the following passage carefully. Then answer the questions below in your own words. You are strongly advised to read the entire text before attempting the questions.

**How AIDS Began**

Never throw anything away that you do not want, you don't know when it might become useful. In 1959 a man living in the then Belgian Congo (now the Democratic Republic of Congo) gave a blood sample to some American doctors who were studying human genetics. When they had finished with it, instead of dropping it in a rubbish bin, the doctors put it in a freezer, where it hung around half forgotten, until 1986. In that year, Andre Nahmias of Emory University, in Atlanta, examined it along with 1212 similar samples. Dr. Nahmias was looking for signs of Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), the cause of the newly recognised disease AIDS. The sample proved positive, showing that AIDS, or at least HIV, had long predated the so-called "patient 0", an airline cabin attendant whose promiscuous peregrinations across North America helped the disease to get a good grip there before it was recognised by doctors.

Surprisingly, considering the controversy that surrounds the origins of AIDS (popular conspiracy theories include the idea that it escaped from a military laboratory in a country of your choice, or that it is part of a western racist plot to reduce the population of Africa, or that it piggy-backed around on an early polio vaccine), that early sample has only just been re-examined to find out if more can be learned. The main idea is to see if there is any indication of where the virus actually came from. This work was carried out by Dr. Nahmias, as well as David Ho, the leader of the team, and Tuofo Zhu of the Aaron Diamond AIDS Research Centre in New York.

The results, published this week in Nature, confirm the prevailing scientific consensus that HIV is a virus which has hopped, or jumped, over the "species barrier" and into mankind from another animal. But they suggest that the hop took place longer ago than has been suspected. They also suggest that for the form of AIDS which is now spreading world-wide, this hop or jump only took place once. In other words, there was a true "patient zero". He was not, however, the world's most notorious steward, but rather an anonymous African who somehow, and in some manner that will probably remain forever unknown, tangled with a chimpanzee and came away with more than he had bargained for.

Viruses are little more than genetic material, usually wrapped in a protein coat. Generally the genetic material involved is DNA, the molecule that also carries the genes in animals, plants, and bacteria. HIV, however, is exceptional. It belongs to an aberrant class of virus known as the retroviruses, which package their genes in the form of DNA's sister molecule, RNA.

It became evident long ago that there were two forms of AIDS, caused by two different, though related, viruses. These are known as HIV-1 and HIV-2. The global AIDS epidemic is caused by HIV-1; fortunately for everybody except for those who live there, HIV-2 is more or less confined to West Africa. Dr. Nahmias' sample was known as ZR59, after Zaire, as the country was then known.

Around a year after the sample was collected, Congo erupted into one of the bloodiest civil wars in African History. War, and the refugees and starvation which result from it, provide ideal circumstances for any disease to spread. And the activities of armies composed of young men are particularly likely to give infection a boost. Without civil war, HIV-1 might, like its cousin HIV-2, still be confined to a small area of Africa.

*(Culled from The Economist, February 7th 1998)*

**Questions**

1. What were American doctors doing with blood samples in 1959 in Belgian Congo? (2 marks)

2. Why are there popular conspiracy theories about the origins of AIDS? (1 mark)

3. How do scientists, in the opinion of the author, explain the presence of HIV in humans? (1 mark)

4. What do you think was the belief about the role of the so-called notorious airline steward? (1 mark)

5. In what way might HIV be different from other viruses? (1 mark)

6. Explain, in your own words, how the civil war in Congo helped spread the HIV virus. (1 mark)

7. Do you think that the opinion of the author about the origin of AIDS is acceptable? Justify your answer. (2 marks)

**Question concernée : n°1 (2 marks).**

### Rappel de méthode
Une question de compréhension se répond en reformulant un passage précis du texte, jamais par une impression générale non appuyée sur le passage. Sur un texte scientifique de vulgarisation comme celui-ci, il faut distinguer soigneusement ce que le texte présente comme un fait établi (les résultats publiés dans Nature) de ce qu'il présente comme une simple croyance populaire ou une hypothèse (les théories du complot, la légende du « patient zéro »).

En 1959, des médecins américains étudiaient la génétique humaine et, dans ce cadre, ont recueilli un échantillon de sang auprès d'un homme vivant alors au Congo belge. Une fois leur étude terminée, au lieu de jeter cet échantillon, ils l'ont congelé, où il est resté oublié pendant près de trente ans, jusqu'à sa réanalyse en 1986.

1. What were American doctors doing with blood samples in 1959 in Belgian Congo? (2 marks)

2. Why are there popular conspiracy theories about the origins of AIDS? (1 mark)

3. How do scientists, in the opinion of the author, explain the presence of HIV in humans? (1 mark)

4. What do you think was the belief about the role of the so-called notorious airline steward? (1 mark)

5. In what way might HIV be different from other viruses? (1 mark)

6. Explain, in your own words, how the civil war in Congo helped spread the HIV virus. (1 mark)

7. Do you think that the opinion of the author about the origin of AIDS is acceptable? Justify your answer. (2 marks)

**Question concernée : n°7 (2 marks).**

**Réponse personnelle argumentée (exemple de réponse recevable) :** L'opinion de l'auteur me paraît globalement acceptable, car elle s'appuie sur une étude scientifique publiée dans une revue reconnue (Nature) et sur des chercheurs identifiés, plutôt que sur une simple spéculation comme les théories du complot mentionnées plus haut. L'auteur reste par ailleurs prudent, reconnaissant que certains détails (comment exactement l'homme est entré en contact avec le chimpanzé) resteront probablement toujours inconnus, ce qui rend son propos plus crédible qu'une affirmation catégorique.

### Piège à éviter
Cette question invite à une opinion personnelle argumentée, pas à un simple résumé du texte : il faut expliquer pourquoi on trouve l'explication de l'auteur convaincante ou non, pas seulement répéter ce que dit le texte.

### Conseil
Pour justifier une opinion sur la fiabilité d'une explication scientifique, appuie-toi sur des critères concrets présents dans le texte lui-même (source de l'information, prudence ou excès de certitude de l'auteur, existence de preuves citées) plutôt que sur une impression générale.
